content: Cardiomegaly is defined as an enlargement of the heart beyond its normal size. It is most commonly identified on a chest X-ray and less frequently during routine physical examinations. Cardiomegaly may serve as the initial indication of an underlying systemic or cardiovascular disease. The pathophysiology of cardiomegaly involves two primary processes affecting the heart muscle: hypertrophy and dilation. Hypertrophy refers to the thickening of the cardiac muscle, leading to an increase in heart size. Dilation, on the other hand, results from the stretching of the heart muscle, typically due to volume overload within the heart. There are numerous potential causes of cardiomegaly, including the use of certain medications, genetic conditions, endocrine disorders, infectious processes, exposure to toxins, and iatrogenic factors. Differentiating cardiomegaly from other diseases requires careful consideration, as it is a finding associated with many conditions. The differential diagnosis can be refined by identifying the specific heart chamber affected and determining whether the enlargement is due to dilation or hypertrophy. Additional physical findings, imaging studies, and laboratory results are essential in identifying the underlying cause of the heart enlargement. The patient’s history and symptoms can provide valuable clues to the underlying cause of cardiomegaly. For instance, a history of rheumatic heart disease, congenital heart disease, or alcohol abuse may suggest dilated cardiomyopathy. Symptoms such as chest pain or other cardiac and respiratory complaints can also help elucidate the cause. A thorough physical examination, including a detailed cardiac assessment, is critical in identifying cardiomegaly and may provide insights into the nature of the underlying condition. The patient’s body habitus should be considered when interpreting findings during the cardiac examination. Laboratory tests that are commonly performed in cases of suspected or confirmed cardiomegaly include a complete blood count, thyroid-stimulating hormone levels, and blood urea nitrogen levels. These tests are high-yield and can provide important diagnostic information. Additional tests may be ordered based on clinical suspicion derived from the patient’s history and physical examination. An electrocardiogram (EKG) is a standard diagnostic tool for evaluating patients with cardiomegaly. It can help determine the cause, severity, and the specific heart chamber involved. For example, the presence of a Q wave may indicate myocardial necrosis contributing to the enlargement, while ST elevation may suggest myocardial infarction, myocarditis, or pericarditis. Cardiomegaly is readily visualized on a chest X-ray, particularly on a posteroanterior (PA) film. Other findings on the chest X-ray can help identify the specific heart chamber contributing most significantly to the enlargement. An echocardiogram is recommended for patients suspected of having valvular disease, abnormal chamber size, ventricular dysfunction, or wall motion abnormalities. This imaging modality provides detailed information about the structure and function of the heart. Other diagnostic studies, such as exercise or pharmacologic stress testing, may be indicated in patients suspected of having coronary artery disease. In cases where valvular disease or coronary artery disease is suspected, cardiac catheterization may be necessary for a comprehensive evaluation following echocardiography. Treatment of cardiomegaly involves both acute and chronic pharmacologic therapies. Chronic management typically includes diuretics and ACE inhibitors. Acute therapies may involve the use of digoxin, diuretics, antiarrhythmic medications, and agents that reduce pre-load and after-load. In patients with end-stage symptomatic heart failure who are awaiting transplantation, implantable ventricular assist devices may serve as a temporary measure to support cardiac function. In select cases, heart transplantation may be considered as a definitive treatment option.
